summary: This unit teaches you to choose, check, use and look after the power tools of electrical installation work, and to lead a team that uses them safely. You will learn to plan tool use for a job and to pick the right tool for drilling, coring, chasing, cutting, hole-making, threading, crimping and fixing. You will also learn to control the hazards: electric shock, hidden services, kickback, dust, noise, vibration, fire and falling tools, and to carry out the checks, inspections, battery care, maintenance and records that keep tools safe.

blocks.p: An electrician spends much of the day with a power tool in hand: drilling fixings, coring walls, cutting strut, making holes in enclosures, crimping lugs. Used well, these tools make neat work quickly. Used badly, they injure people, damage buildings and spoil the installation. This Level 3 unit goes beyond using a drill: you must plan which tools a job needs, choose the best method, control the health risks for your whole team, and make sure every tool is fit for use.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Plan tool use for a job
Survey the job, write the risk assessment and method, and plan tools, power supply, access, dust and noise control, permits and PPE.
Choose the right tool
Pick the tool, bit, blade or disc that does each task safely and neatly, and explain why.
Supply tools safely
Use GFCI or RCD protection, leads of the right rating, and tools that suit Jamaica's 110 V or 220 V, 50 Hz supply.
Check tools
Carry out the user check before every use, know what formal inspection and testing covers, and take faulty tools out of use.
Drill, core and chase
Use rotary hammers, core drills and wall chasers correctly, after checking for hidden services.
Cut, make holes and fix
Use grinders, band saws, reciprocating saws, hole saws, step drills, knockout punches, drill-drivers, impact drivers and torque tools properly.
Use hydraulic and specialist tools
Crimp lugs, cut cable, thread and bend conduit, and know who may use cartridge tools.
Control health hazards
Control dust, noise and vibration, choose PPE and prevent falling tools.
Care for tools and batteries
Clean, store and maintain tools, look after lithium-ion batteries and keep the tool register.
Lead the team
Check training, demonstrate, supervise, correct unsafe habits and report incidents.

ul: JPS supplies **110 V and 220 V at 50 Hz**. Most portable tools here are 110–120 V; some larger machines are 220 V. Check the rating plate against the outlet every time.

On British sites, '110 V' means a special reduced-voltage supply from a site transformer, with only 55 V to earth. **Jamaica's 110 V is the ordinary mains**, with the full 110 V to ground. It is not a safety voltage, so GFCI or RCD protection matters.

Many tools are bought from North America, where the supply is 60 Hz. Check that the rating plate says **50 Hz or 50/60 Hz**. Tools with brush motors (most hand-held drills, grinders and saws) usually run well on 50 Hz, but machines with induction motors and some chargers may run slow or overheat. If the plate says 60 Hz only, ask the maker.
Heat, humidity and salt air are hard on tools. Store them dry, keep batteries out of hot vehicles, and wipe tools down after work near the sea.

blocks.note: Read the maker's instructions for every tool you use or issue. Figures in this kit are typical; the maker's instructions, your risk assessment and your instructor come first.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Read the sections in order: planning and choosing first, then electrical safety and checks, then each group of tools, then health hazards and leadership. Try the practice test and read every explanation. Your instructor will demonstrate each tool and watch you use it before you use it alone.

sections.title: Planning tool use for a job

blocks.p: Before any power tool comes out of the van, plan the work. Most power-tool accidents and most complaints about dust and noise come from jobs that were never planned.

flow: Visit the site and study the drawings
List the tasks: holes, chases, cuts, fixings, terminations
Check for hidden services and structural limits
Choose the tool and method for each task
Plan the power supply, access, dust and noise control and PPE
Arrange permits and agree times with the client
Check the tools are inspected and the team is trained
Write the risk assessment and method statement; brief the team

head: Question
Think about
rows: What are we drilling or cutting into?
Block, concrete, reinforced or post-tensioned concrete, steel, plasterboard, tile. Structural members need the engineer's approval before coring or chasing.
What is hidden inside it?
Cables, water and gas pipes, reinforcing steel. Check drawings, look at where outlets and pipes are, and scan.
Where is the power coming from?
Which outlets, their voltage and rating, GFCI protection, lead lengths; or cordless tools; or a generator.
How will we reach the work?
A platform or tower, not the top of a ladder, for heavy drilling; tool lanyards at height; the area below fenced off.
Who else is affected?
Occupants, other trades, the public. Plan noisy and dusty work for quiet times; put up barriers and signs.
What about dust, noise and vibration?
Extraction, water, respirators, hearing protection, sharing the work between people.
Is there a fire risk?
Sparks from grinders need a hot-work permit, a fire watch and an extinguisher. Choose a cold-cutting tool if you can.
Who may use each tool?
Only people trained on it. Core drills, threading machines and cartridge tools need specific training.
Are the tools fit for use?
Formal inspection in date, user checks done, the right bits and blades, sharp and undamaged.

blocks.note: The safest and neatest hole is often the one you do not make. Before planning chases and cores, ask whether surface conduit or trunking, an existing duct, or a different route would do the job.

blocks.p: **SDS** is the chuck system on rotary hammers: the bit's grooved shank slides in and locks without a key, and can move back and forth for the hammer action. SDS-plus is the common size for bits up to about 26–30 mm; SDS-max is a larger shank for heavy tools and big bits.

blocks.note: Do not make one tool do another's job. A grinding disc used on edge to cut, an impact driver on a terminal, or a hammer drill forced through reinforced concrete all end in damage or injury.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Electrical safety and power for tools

ul: Run every corded tool through a **GFCI or RCD**. If the outlet has none, plug a portable GFCI into the outlet first, so that it protects the lead as well as the tool, and press its TEST button before work.
If the GFCI trips when a tool starts, especially on a damp morning, **stop using the tool and lead and have them checked**. Never bypass the device or keep resetting it.

A **Class I** tool has a metal case and a three-pin plug: its safety depends on the grounding pin and conductor. A **Class II** (double-insulated) tool is marked with a square inside a square and has no grounding conductor.
Keep leads out of water, off sharp edges and away from the blade or bit.
With wet tools such as wet core drills, follow the maker's instructions on GFCI protection exactly, and keep water away from the motor.

blocks.h: Will the lead and the circuit carry the load?

blocks.p: For a tool, **current = power ÷ voltage** (I = P ÷ V). The current must not be more than the rating of the lead, the plug, the outlet or the circuit.

head: Tool rating
On 110 V
On 220 V
rows: 800 W drill
1 100 W rotary hammer
5 A
1 650 W wall chaser
2 200 W core drill

ul: On 110 V a tool draws **twice the current** it would on 220 V for the same power, so leads must be heavier and voltage drop is greater.
Add up everything on one lead or multi-outlet box. A 1 100 W rotary hammer and a 1 200 W vacuum together draw 2 300 ÷ 110 = about 21 A: too much for a 13 A or 15 A lead or a 20 A circuit.
A long, thin lead causes **voltage drop**: the tool runs slow, loses power and overheats. Use the shortest lead that reaches, with a conductor size suited to the current.
**Unwind a cable reel fully** under heavy load. A coiled lead cannot lose its heat and can melt.
Do not plug one extension lead into another.

blocks.p: On sites with no supply, a portable generator may power the tools. Use one with GFCI-protected outlets or add a portable GFCI, follow the maker's instructions for grounding, run it outdoors away from doors and windows because of exhaust fumes, and never connect it to a building's wiring through an outlet.

blocks.note: A tool rated 110–120 V must never be plugged into a 220 V outlet, and plugs must not be changed or adapted to make it fit. If the rating plate and the outlet do not match, the tool is not used there.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: The user check before every use

blocks.p: Do it with the plug out or the battery off. It takes a minute.

head: Part
Look for
rows: Plug
Cracks, burn marks, bent or loose pins, a missing grounding pin, tape repairs

Cuts, crushing, kinks or tape along its whole length; the sheath held firmly where it enters the plug and the tool

Cracks, missing screws, side handle fitted and tight

Fitted, undamaged and adjusted

Works, springs back when released, lock-on not stuck

Clear of dust
Inspection label
Formal inspection and test in date
Battery (cordless)

GFCI or RCD

Unplug it or remove the battery
Tag it 'DO NOT USE' with the fault, date and your name
Put it apart from good tools
Report it and record it in the tool register

blocks.p: As well as the user's check, each portable tool and lead is formally inspected and tested at set intervals by a competent person. This is needed because **some faults cannot be seen**: a broken grounding conductor inside a lead looks perfect from outside.

head: Point
User check
Formal inspection and test
rows: Who
The user
A competent person with a suitable tester
When
Before every use
At the interval the firm's procedure sets: on building sites often every few months; less often for tools used in offices
What
Looking and trying the switch
A closer inspection, including inside the plug, and electrical tests
Tests
GFCI test button only
Earth (ground) continuity from the casing to the plug's grounding pin on Class I tools; insulation resistance; polarity of leads; a run test
Record
Tool check sheet where the firm uses one
The result in the register and a dated label on the tool

blocks.p: A Class II tool has no grounding conductor, so it has no earth continuity test: its insulation is tested instead. Passing the formal test does not replace the user check: a lead can be cut the day after it was tested.

head: The user may
A competent repairer does
rows: Wipe the tool clean and blow or brush dust from the vents, with the plug out
Replace a damaged lead or plug
Change bits, blades and discs with the plug out or the battery removed
Open the casing or motor; replace brushes, switches and bearings
Lightly grease the shank of an SDS bit, to reduce wear on the bit and chuck
Repair or adjust hydraulic tools; recalibrate torque tools
Sharpen or replace blunt bits and blades
Carry out the formal inspection and test
Check and tighten handles and guards
Anything the maker's instructions reserve for a service agent

ul: Blunt bits and blades need more force, run hotter, vibrate more and take longer. Replace them.
Store tools clean and dry in their cases, with leads loosely coiled, not wrapped tightly round the tool.
Torque tools are measuring instruments: they need calibration, and they are set back to their lowest setting after use if the maker says so.

blocks.p: Each tool has a number and an entry in the register: what it is, who has it, its inspection dates and its repairs. Tools are **signed out and signed back in**, with a post-use check, so that a missing or damaged tool is noticed the same day and can be traced to the job where it happened.

ul: Check the drawings, but do not trust them alone.
Look at both sides of the wall: where are the outlets, switches, pipes and boards? Cables usually run to them, but not always in straight lines.
Scan with a cable and pipe detector, and with a rebar scanner on structural concrete. Know your detector's limits: depth, plastic pipes, and cables carrying no current.
Before coring a floor slab, find out what is below it and fence that area off.

**Post-tensioned slabs** contain steel tendons under great tension. Cutting one can be deadly and can wreck the structure. Never drill or core one without the structural engineer's written approval and a marked safe position.
Treat any cable you find as live until it is isolated and proved dead.

flow: Select the mode: hammer drilling for concrete and block; rotation only for tile, timber and steel
Wipe and lightly grease the bit's shank; push it in until it locks; pull to check
Fit the side handle; set the depth stop
Stand balanced, both hands on the tool, clear of the lead
Start slowly on the mark, then run up to speed
Let the tool do the work with steady pressure; withdraw now and then to clear dust
If the bit jams or hits steel, release the trigger at once

ul: **Hammer off** for tiles, timber and steel: the blows would crack tile and do nothing useful in wood or metal. For a tiled wall, drill the tile on rotation only, then switch the hammer on for the wall behind.
Set the **depth stop** so that a fixing hole is deep enough for the plug or anchor but does not break through or hit what is behind.

**Kickback** is the sudden, violent twist of the tool when the bit binds. The side handle, a firm stance and the tool's **slip clutch** (which lets the motor slip when the bit jams) protect your wrists. Never remove the side handle 'because it gets in the way'.
If the bit hits **reinforcing steel**, stop. Do not force it or switch to a bigger tool. Move the hole within what the drawing allows, or ask: steel must not be cut without the engineer's approval.

**Overhead**: work from a stable platform at a comfortable height, not at full stretch or from the top of a stepladder. Use extraction or a dust cup, wear eye protection, and keep people out from below.

blocks.p: An anchor only holds its rated load if it is installed as the maker says: the right hole diameter and depth, the **hole cleaned out** with a blow-out pump and brush (dust left in the hole greatly reduces the grip, especially of resin anchors), the right distance from edges and other anchors, and tightening to the stated torque. Heavy items overhead, such as cable tray and ladder, depend on this.

head: Type
Used with
Notes
rows: TCT (tungsten carbide) core bit
A rotary hammer, for holes in block and brick
Has a pilot drill; follow the maker on hammer action; not for reinforced concrete
Dry diamond core bit
A core drill or a suitable drill on **rotation only**, with dust extraction
Brick, block and some concrete; hammer action destroys the diamond segments
Wet diamond core bit
A core drill on a **stand**, with water fed to the cut
Hard and reinforced concrete; water cools the bit and stops dust

flow: Check drawings, scan, and get approval for the hole
Check the drill, bit, leads and GFCI protection
Mark the centre; fence off the far side or the area below
Fix the stand firmly by the anchor or vacuum base the maker recommends, square to the surface
Arrange to collect the water and slurry; protect what is nearby
Start slowly, then feed steadily without forcing
If the bit binds, stop and free it; never fight it
Remove the core safely; clean up the slurry

blocks.note: A large core bit that jams will turn the machine instead. Hand-held coring is only for small bits on tools with a safety clutch, held by both handles; anything larger goes on a stand. Wet coring mixes water and electricity: use the GFCI protection the maker specifies, keep connections dry and wear rubber-soled boots.
blocks.label: Safety

ul: A **wall chaser** has two diamond blades side by side. Set the width and depth, connect the extraction vacuum, cut both lines in one pass, then chisel out the strip between them.
Always use the extractor: chasing makes more dust than any other electrical task.

Keep chases as shallow and short as the conduit allows. Deep or long horizontal chases weaken a wall; a common rule for block walls is no deeper than one-third of the wall's thickness for vertical chases and one-sixth for horizontal ones, but the engineer's or the building code's limits apply.
Do not chase structural columns, beams or lintels.

sections.title: Cutting, making holes and fixing in metal and boards

ul: Use the right disc: a thin **cutting disc** for cutting, a thicker **grinding disc** for grinding. Never grind with the side of a cutting disc or cut with a grinding disc on edge.
The disc's **maximum speed** (rpm) marked on it must be at least the grinder's speed, and its diameter and bore must fit the tool. Check the expiry date and look for cracks or chips.
The **guard** stays on, positioned between you and the disc. Fit the side handle and use both hands.
**Clamp the work.** Support it so that the cut opens as you go; if the cut closes and pinches the disc, the grinder kicks back.
Let the disc reach full speed before it touches the work, and let it stop before you put the grinder down.

Grinding and cutting are **hot work**: sparks travel several metres and can smoulder for a long time. Where anything can burn, arrange a hot-work permit, clear or cover combustibles, keep an extinguisher at hand and keep a fire watch during the work and for the time the permit sets afterwards, often 30 to 60 minutes.
PPE: eye and face protection, hearing protection, gloves and non-flammable clothing.

head: Saw
Key points
rows: Portable band saw

Clamp or firmly support the work; choose a blade with at least three teeth in the material's thickness; both hands on the handles; let the saw's weight feed the cut; keep fingers clear of the blade; deburr the cut end
Reciprocating saw
Hold the **shoe firmly against the work**: this stops the saw jumping and the blade bending or snapping; choose the blade for the material; check what is behind the cut
Jigsaw
Sole flat on the work; the blade must be clear below; for curved and internal cuts in sheet
Oscillating multi-tool
The blade moves a few degrees from side to side at high speed; ideal for plunge cuts in plasterboard and trimming in tight places; set the depth so you do not cut cables behind the board

blocks.h: Holes in steel enclosures and trunking

head: Method
Best for
Points
rows: Step drill
Holes up to about 30 mm in sheet
One bit gives many sizes; stop at the right step; low speed
Hole saw (bi-metal)
Larger round holes
Pilot drill first; **low speed**, steady feed and cutting oil on steel; work held firmly. Snagging and jerking usually mean the speed is too high or the work is moving
Knockout punch (hand or hydraulic)
Clean, exact holes for glands and conduit fittings
Drill a pilot hole for the draw stud; the punch shears the hole with no sparks and almost no swarf
Angle grinder
Never for round holes
It leaves a rough, wrong-shaped opening and showers the inside with sparks and grit

blocks.p: **Drill speed.** The larger the bit and the harder the material, the slower the speed. A 4 mm bit in aluminium can run fast; a 20 mm hole in steel needs the lowest gear, firm pressure and cutting oil. Too fast burns the bit's edge blue and blunts it in seconds.

ul: **Swarf** (metal chips) conducts. Left in an enclosure, it can cause a short circuit or track across insulation months later.
Wherever possible, make holes before devices are fitted.

If breakers or other devices are already inside, the board must be **isolated, locked off and proved dead**; cover the devices, catch the swarf, and vacuum the enclosure afterwards. Never blow swarf out with air.
Deburr every hole and cut end so that cables and hands are not cut.
On a drill-driver, set the **clutch** low and raise it until the screw seats without stripping. Use the drill setting only for drilling.
Use an impact driver for long screws and self-drilling screws, never for terminals, accessory screws or anything with a stated torque.

Tighten every breaker terminal, neutral bar, lug and busbar joint with a **torque tool set to the maker's figure**. A loose connection overheats; an over-tightened one cracks the terminal or crushes the conductor.
These fire a hardened pin into concrete or steel with an explosive cartridge. **Only a person trained and authorised** on that tool may use it.

Never fire into very hard or brittle materials (glazed tile, cast iron, hardened steel), into thin or hollow materials, close to an edge, or into an existing hole: the pin can ricochet or pass straight through, and the base material can shatter.
Choose the cartridge strength the maker gives for the pin and material, starting with the weakest; the strengths are colour-coded.
Wear eye and hearing protection, keep others away, hold the tool square and hard against the surface, and follow the maker's misfire procedure exactly.
Keep the tool unloaded until the moment of use, and keep tool and cartridges locked away.

blocks.p: Large cable lugs are compressed onto the conductor by a hand or battery hydraulic tool. A good crimp is as strong and as conductive as the cable; a bad one overheats under load.

flow: Confirm the cable is a new end, or is isolated and proved dead
Match the lug to the conductor size and material (copper or aluminium) and to the stud size
Select the die marked for that lug, from the tool maker's chart
Strip the insulation to the length of the lug's barrel without nicking the strands
Push the conductor fully into the barrel
Position the lug in the die as the maker shows; keep fingers out of the jaws
Run the tool through its full cycle until it releases
Make the number of crimps the maker states, in the stated order
Inspect the crimp

head: Check on the finished crimp
Why
rows: The die code or size is stamped clearly into the barrel
Shows the right die was used and the cycle was completed
The conductor is visible at the inspection hole or the end of the barrel
Shows it was fully inserted
No strands outside the barrel, none cut
All the copper is carrying current
No insulation inside the barrel
Insulation under the crimp gives a loose, high-resistance joint
No cracks; no sharp flash left on the barrel
Cracks mean the wrong die or lug
The lug cannot be pulled or twisted on the cable
A firm pull test

blocks.note: Hydraulic jaws close with a force of several tonnes and do not stop for a finger. Hold the lug by the cable or the palm, never between the dies, and keep your other hand away when you trigger the tool. Do not use a tool that leaks oil or fails to complete its cycle.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: Ratchet and hydraulic cutters cut large cables cleanly. Before cutting any existing cable, **identify it at both ends and prove it dead**; a cable in a group can easily be mistaken for its neighbour. If a cable cannot be positively identified, stop and tell your supervisor: specialist methods exist and are for authorised people only. Never cut steel wire armour or steel rope with cutters made for copper and aluminium.

flow: Check guards, foot switch, lead and GFCI protection; set the machine on firm, level ground
Support long conduit on a stand so that it cannot whip or tip
Cut the conduit square and ream the bore to remove the burr
Fit and set the die head for the conduit size and thread length
Check that cutting oil is flowing over the dies
Grip the conduit in the chuck; run the machine from the foot switch and cut the thread
Open the die head, stop the machine, remove the conduit
Wipe off the oil, try the thread with a coupler, and clear the swarf with a brush

ul: **Cutting oil** cools the dies and gives a clean, sharp thread; cutting dry tears the thread and ruins the dies.
The **foot switch** stops the machine the moment your foot lifts, so you can stop it at once if clothing or a hand is caught. Never wedge it down or leave the machine running unattended.
Keep loose sleeves, gloves, jewellery and long hair away from the turning chuck and conduit. Handle swarf with a brush, not your fingers: it is razor sharp.
Stand clear of the turning end of a long length.
Hydraulic and machine benders: use the former (shoe) for the conduit size, mark the bend first, keep hands out of the pinch points and stand clear of the moving conduit end.

Heat guns for heat-shrink sleeving: the nozzle and the work stay hot enough to burn skin and start fires; keep them moving, keep them away from cable insulation you do not mean to heat, and rest the gun on its stand to cool.

sections.title: Health hazards, PPE and leading the team

blocks.p: Concrete, block, mortar and tile contain **crystalline silica**. Drilling, chasing and cutting turn it into dust fine enough to reach deep into the lungs, often too fine to see. Over years it causes **silicosis**, which scars the lungs and cannot be cured, and it is linked to lung cancer and other lung disease. Control it in this order:

ol: **Make less dust**: fewer chases, surface containment, routes that need fewer holes.
**Capture it at the tool**: on-tool extraction connected to a vacuum made for fine construction dust, or water where the tool is made for it.
**Keep others away**: close doors, screen the area, put up signs, work when the building is empty.
**Wear a respirator**: a close-fitting one of the rating the risk assessment gives (for example N95 or P2 as a minimum, higher for chasing), fitted properly. It cannot seal over a beard or stubble.
**Clean up with the vacuum**. Never dry sweep or blow dust with compressed air: both put it back into the air.
**Share the dusty work** so that no one person does it all day.

ul: Rotary hammers, chasers, grinders and cartridge tools are loud enough to damage hearing, typically 95 to 105 dB(A) or more at the user's ear. Damage is painless, builds up and is permanent.
As a guide, if you must shout to be heard by someone 1 m away, hearing protection is needed.
Controls: quieter methods and sharp bits; less time exposed; hearing protection (both ears, properly fitted) for everyone in the area; signs; and noisy work timed for when others are away.

blocks.p: Regular use of hammering and rotary tools can cause **hand-arm vibration syndrome**: tingling and numbness in the fingers, fingers that turn white in the cold, and loss of grip. It is permanent if it is allowed to develop.

Makers state each tool's vibration level in m/s². Under the European and British rules, which are a sound guide where there is no local figure, action must be taken when daily exposure reaches 2.5 m/s² averaged over 8 hours, and the limit is 5 m/s². The time a tool can be used before reaching the action level is **8 hours × (2.5 ÷ the tool's vibration level)²**.

ul: Choose lower-vibration tools and methods; keep bits and blades sharp.
Share the work so that no one uses the chaser or rotary hammer all day.
Let the tool do the work: do not grip harder or push harder than needed.
Take breaks and keep hands warm and dry.
Anyone with tingling, numbness or white fingers must report it at once.

head: Work
PPE
rows: Any power tool
Safety glasses; safety boots; close-fitting clothing; long hair tied back; no jewellery
Drilling and chasing masonry
Add hearing protection and a fitted dust respirator
Grinding and cutting metal
Add a face shield or goggles, hearing protection, gloves and non-flammable clothing
Handling cut metal, sheet and swarf
Cut-resistant gloves
Rotating machines: threading machines, bench drills
No loose gloves, sleeves or ties near the moving parts
Wet coring
Waterproof boots and gloves as the maker advises

ul: Work from a platform or tower with guard rails and toe boards, not from the top of a ladder.
Tether tools with **tool lanyards** rated for their weight, so that a dropped tool cannot hit someone below.
Fence off the area underneath and put up signs.
Pass tools up in a bag or on a line; never throw them.
Use only the charger and batteries made for the tool. Do not use adaptors between makes.
Carry spare batteries with their terminal covers on, away from loose screws, bits and other metal that could short the terminals.

Do not use or charge a battery that is cracked, swollen, leaking, has been dropped hard or gets hot. Put it somewhere safe, outdoors and away from anything that burns, and report it for proper disposal. Never put batteries in ordinary rubbish or a fire.
Charge on a hard, non-flammable surface, in a cool, ventilated place, within the temperature range the maker gives. Do not charge in a closed vehicle or site container in the sun.
Let a hot battery cool before charging, and do not leave batteries on charge unattended overnight unless the maker's system is designed for it.

flow: Find out what each person is trained and authorised to use
For a new tool: explain, demonstrate, then watch them use it on a practice piece
Brief the team each day on the method, hazards and site rules
Check that tools are inspected and that GFCI protection is in place
Watch the work; correct unsafe habits at once and explain why
Have tools cleaned, checked and signed back in
Report and discuss every incident and near miss

blocks.p: After any incident, such as a kickback injury, a drill striking a cable or a disc breaking: stop the work and make the area safe; treat any struck cable and the tool as live until the circuit is isolated, locked off and proved dead; give first aid and have anyone who may have had a shock checked by a doctor; take the tool out of use for inspection; report it; then find out why it happened and change the method so that it does not happen again. Brief the whole team on what was learned.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can plan the use of power tools for a job, including supply, access, hidden services, dust, noise, permits and PPE.
I can choose the best tool for drilling, coring, chasing, cutting, hole-making, threading, crimping and tightening, and explain my choice.
I can explain the difference between a drill-driver, a combi drill, a rotary hammer and an impact driver.
I can work out a tool's current and decide whether a lead and circuit can carry it.
I can explain why Jamaica's 110 V is not a reduced safety voltage, and why a tool's rating plate must be checked for voltage and frequency.
I can carry out a user check, say what formal inspection and testing adds, and take a faulty tool out of use.
I can check for hidden services before drilling or coring.
I can use a rotary hammer correctly: mode, side handle, depth stop, stance, and what to do when the bit jams.
I can describe how to set up a diamond core drill and a wall chaser safely.
I can choose and check an angle grinder disc and explain hot-work precautions.
I can make clean holes in an enclosure and keep swarf out of equipment.
I can make and inspect a hydraulic crimp, and thread conduit safely.
I can control dust, noise and vibration for my team, and estimate vibration exposure time.
I can look after lithium-ion batteries.
I can train, supervise and correct trainees, keep the tool register and report incidents.

What it is

Tool current: 1 100 W on 110 V is 10 A
110 V and 220 V, 50 Hz
The JPS supply; check the tool's rating plate
About 95 to 105 dB(A)

terms: Anchor
A fixing set into a drilled hole in concrete or masonry to carry a load.
Class I tool
A tool with a metal case that relies on a grounding conductor for safety.
Class II tool
A double-insulated tool, marked with a square inside a square, with no grounding conductor.
Clutch
The adjustable ring on a drill-driver that slips at a set tightness; also the safety clutch in a rotary hammer that slips when the bit jams.
Core bit
A hollow tube with cutting segments on its end, for large round holes in masonry and concrete.
Depth stop
A rod on a drill that limits how deep the bit can go.
Die
The shaped part of a crimping tool that forms the crimp, or the cutter in a threading machine.
Hand-arm vibration syndrome
Permanent damage to the nerves and blood vessels of the hands from vibrating tools.
Hot work
Work that makes sparks, flame or heat that could start a fire, such as grinding.
Kickback
The sudden, violent twist or jump of a tool when its bit, blade or disc binds.
Knockout punch
A tool that shears a clean round hole in sheet metal with a punch and die drawn together.
Lanyard (tool tether)
A cord that ties a tool to the worker or platform so that it cannot fall.
Oscillating multi-tool
A tool whose blade moves rapidly from side to side, for plunge cuts and trimming.
Rotary hammer
A drill with a piston-driven hammer action and an SDS chuck, for concrete and masonry.
SDS
The slotted-shank chuck system used on rotary hammers.
Silica
A mineral in concrete, block and tile whose fine dust causes silicosis.
Step drill
A cone-shaped bit with steps of increasing diameter, for holes in sheet metal.
Swarf
The metal chips and curls made by drilling and cutting metal.
Tool register
The record of each tool, who has it, and its inspections and repairs.
Torque
Turning force; the tightness to which a screw or bolt is fastened.
Wall chaser
A tool with two diamond blades side by side that cuts slots in walls for conduit and cable.

c1.title: Cable tray on a supermarket soffit in Constant Spring
c1.text: Javier Ellis's team is fixing 60 m of cable tray to the concrete soffit of a supermarket in Constant Spring, St Andrew, while the shop is open. They work from a mobile tower, drilling 12 mm holes with a rotary hammer for drop-in anchors. The anchor maker's instructions say to blow out and brush each hole before setting the anchor. Halfway through one hole, the bit hits steel and stops cutting.

c2.title: Power for tools at a guest house in Moneague
c2.text: Kerone Smith's team is chasing walls in an old guest house in Moneague, St Ann. The nearest outlet is a 110 V outlet on a 15 A circuit. Kerone plans to run a 1 400 W wall chaser and its 1 100 W extraction vacuum from one extension reel rated 13 A. Later in the job he wants to use a bench-mounted band saw that the owner bought in Florida; its rating plate reads '120 V, 60 Hz'.

c3.title: A plant room at a hotel in Oracabessa
c3.text: Shernette Brown's team is fitting out a plant room at a hotel in Oracabessa, St Mary. Two 40 mm holes are needed in the side of an existing distribution board that already has its breakers fitted. A steel bracket must also be trimmed with a 115 mm angle grinder that runs at 11 000 rpm; the only spare cutting disc in the van is marked 'max 8 500 rpm'. While a trainee is cutting the bracket, the offcut sags, the disc jams and the grinder kicks back.

c4.title: The tool store in Porus
c4.text: Ms Hall runs the tool store for a contractor in Porus, Manchester. At Friday's sign-in she finds a cordless drill battery that is slightly swollen and warm. A corded rotary hammer's inspection label shows its next test was due last month. The team has also been charging batteries inside a closed steel site container, which reaches about 45 °C in the afternoon.

c5.title: A trainee on the wall chaser in Frankfield
c5.text: At a community centre in Frankfield, Clarendon, trainee Damion is to cut chases in block walls. The wall chaser's maker gives its vibration level as 8 m/s². Damion has a full beard, and the team's dust respirators are close-fitting half masks. After ten minutes he takes the rotary hammer's side handle off 'because it gets in the way'. A dominoes club uses the next room every afternoon.

questions.q: Which rotary hammer mode should the team use for the 12 mm anchor holes?
o: Rotation only, to protect the concrete
Rotation only at first, then chisel only to finish
Hammer drilling, with rotation
Chisel only, to break the concrete out
questions.why: Concrete is drilled with rotation and hammer action together: the blows break the concrete and the flutes carry the dust out. Rotation only is for tile, timber and steel, and chisel only is for breaking out, not for round holes.

questions.q: Why does the anchor maker say to blow out and brush each hole?
o: Dust left in the hole reduces the anchor's grip
Dust in the hole would blunt the next drill bit
A clean hole lets a smaller anchor be used
Brushing makes the hole slightly deeper
questions.why: An anchor grips the sides of the hole. Loose dust stops it expanding or bonding properly, so it may hold far less than its rated load. Tray overhead in a shop depends on every anchor being set as the maker says.

questions.q: What should the team do about the hole where the bit has hit steel?
o: Leave that anchor out and space the others wider apart
Stop, and move the hole where the design allows
Lean on the drill until it cuts through the bar
Fit a larger bit and drill through at full power
questions.why: The steel is reinforcement, which must not be cut without the engineer's approval; forcing the drill also risks kickback. The hole is moved within what the design allows. Leaving an anchor out overloads the others.

questions.q: Shoppers walk beneath the tower. Which control matters most for them?
o: A helper at the foot of the tower watching the drill
Working faster so the tower is moved on sooner
The area below fenced off, with tools on lanyards
A sign on the tower asking shoppers to take care
questions.why: Keeping people out from under the work removes them from the danger, and lanyards stop a dropped tool falling at all. A sign or a watcher does not stop a drill or a lump of concrete that is already falling.

questions.q: About how much current will the chaser and vacuum draw together?
o: About 13 A
About 2.3 A
About 23 A
About 10 A
questions.why: Total power is 1 400 + 1 100 = 2 500 W, and 2 500 ÷ 110 = 22.7 A. That is far more than the 13 A reel or the 15 A circuit can carry.

questions.q: What should Kerone do about the supply for the chaser and vacuum?
o: Ask for a 30 A breaker to be fitted for that outlet
Use the one reel, as the 15 A breaker will protect the lead
Keep the reel coiled so that the lead stays cooler
Feed them from separate circuits, each with a GFCI
questions.why: Each machine needs a lead and circuit rated for its own current, with GFCI protection. A 15 A breaker does not protect a 13 A lead, a coiled reel overheats, and a bigger breaker on the same cable is a fire risk.

questions.q: What must Kerone find out before using the band saw from Florida?
o: Whether its plug is the two-pin type
Whether its blade has metric or inch teeth
Whether its lead is longer than 2 m
Whether it is suitable for a 50 Hz supply
questions.why: The plate says 60 Hz only. A bench machine may have an induction motor, which runs about one-sixth slower on 50 Hz and can overheat. He should check with the maker or have a competent person assess it before it is used.

questions.q: What is the best way to make the two 40 mm holes in the board?
o: With a rotary hammer and a 40 mm core bit
With the grinder, while the board stays in service
With a hole saw at high speed, to keep the job quick
Board proved dead, devices covered, knockout punch
questions.why: The board must be isolated, locked off and proved dead and its devices covered. A knockout punch shears a clean hole through a small pilot hole with almost no swarf and no sparks. Swarf left in a board can cause a short circuit later.

questions.q: May the disc marked 'max 8 500 rpm' be used on the 11 000 rpm grinder?
o: Yes, if the guard is fitted and the cut is short
Yes, if the trainee does not press too hard
No: the disc could burst at the grinder's speed
No: the disc would turn too slowly to cut
questions.why: A disc must be rated for at least the speed of the tool. Run faster than its marked maximum, it can break apart and throw pieces at high speed. Get a disc of the right size and rating.

questions.q: What most likely caused the grinder to kick back?
o: The disc was too sharp and new for mild steel
The trainee was holding it with both hands
The grinder's guard was fitted too close
The sagging offcut closed the cut on the disc
questions.why: When the work is not supported so that the cut opens, the weight of the offcut closes the cut and pinches the disc, and the grinder is thrown back. Clamp the work and support it so the cut stays open.

questions.q: What should Ms Hall do with the swollen, warm battery?
o: Take it out of use and put it safely outdoors
Issue it only for light work from now on
Put it on charge to see whether it recovers overnight
Tape over the swelling and mark it 'old'
questions.why: A swollen or hot lithium-ion battery is damaged inside and can catch fire. It must not be used or charged. Move it away from anything that burns, and arrange proper disposal; never put it in ordinary rubbish.

questions.q: What should happen to the rotary hammer whose test was due last month?
o: Issue it, as long as the user does the daily check first
Hold it back until it is inspected and tested
Write a new date on its label and issue it
Issue it, but only for use with a GFCI
questions.why: The formal test finds faults the user cannot see, such as a broken grounding conductor. A tool past its date is held back until a competent person has inspected and tested it. Changing the label would be a false record.

questions.q: What should change about the way the team charges its batteries?
o: Charge them only at night, with nobody left on the site
Stack them together so that one charger serves them all
Charge them in a cool, airy place on a hard surface
Leave the container door shut so that dust stays out
questions.why: Lithium-ion batteries must be charged within the maker's temperature range; a container at 45 °C is too hot and shortens their life and raises the fire risk. Charge them in the shade, with air moving, on a surface that will not burn, where someone will notice a problem.

questions.q: About how long can Damion use the chaser in a day before reaching the vibration action level?
o: About 47 minutes
About 2 hours
About 12 minutes
About 3 hours
questions.why: Time = 8 hours × (2.5 ÷ 8)² = 8 × 0.098 = 0.78 hours, about 47 minutes. After that the work should be shared with others or changed, and the 3-hour limit must never be passed.

questions.q: Why is Damion's beard a problem for the dust respirator?
o: It hides the mask's rating from the supervisor
The mask cannot seal, so dust leaks in round it
Dust collects in the beard and blocks the filter
It makes the mask too hot to wear for long
questions.why: A close-fitting mask only works if its edge seals against the skin. Hair breaks the seal and silica dust is drawn in through the gap. Damion needs to be clean-shaven where the mask seals, or to use a type that does not rely on a face seal, such as a powered hood.

questions.q: What should the team leader do when Damion removes the side handle?
o: Take him off power tools for the rest of the job
Stop him, refit it and explain what it is for
Wait until the end of the day to mention it
Let him carry on, since he feels more comfortable
questions.why: The side handle lets the user resist the twist if the bit jams; without it a kickback can sprain or break a wrist. Unsafe habits are corrected at once, with the reason, so that the trainee understands and does not repeat them.

questions.q: How should the chasing be arranged around the dominoes club next door?
o: Ask the club members to wear dust masks that afternoon
Chase in the mornings, with the room closed and signed
Carry on at any time, since the club is in another room
Chase in the afternoons, when there is more light
questions.why: Dust and noise spread beyond the room where the work is done. Doing the chasing when the next room is empty, behind closed doors with signs and extraction, protects people who have no PPE and no part in the job.

questions.q: Which of these holes needs the lowest drill speed?
o: A 20 mm hole in steel plate
A 6 mm pilot hole in steel
A 4 mm hole in a timber batten
A 4 mm hole in aluminium sheet
questions.why: The larger the bit and the harder the material, the slower it must turn, because the cutting edge of a big bit moves much faster at the same rpm. A 20 mm hole in steel needs the lowest gear, firm feed and cutting oil.

questions.q: A drill's rating plate shows a square inside a square. What does that mean for its formal test?
o: It needs no formal testing, since it cannot give a shock
It must be tested at 220 V and not at 110 V
Its casing must be tested for continuity to the plug
No earth continuity test; its insulation is tested
questions.why: The symbol means Class II, double insulated: there is no grounding conductor to test, so the tester checks the insulation instead. It still needs user checks and formal inspection, because damage can defeat the insulation.

questions.q: Which sign suggests that a hydraulic crimp on a 70 mm² copper lug has been made correctly?
o: The die code is stamped in the barrel
The barrel is squeezed down completely flat
A few strands are showing outside the barrel
The insulation is gripped inside the barrel
questions.why: A clear die code shows the right die was used and the tool completed its cycle. The conductor should also be fully inserted, with no strands outside, no insulation under the crimp and no movement on a pull test. A flattened barrel means the wrong die.
